meta.title: Who really said "Not to know what happened before you were born is to be a child forever"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Cicero really wrote it — in Orator (46 BC), section 120. The Latin, the exact locator, and why this English wording’s translator is unidentified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Not to know what happened before you were born is to be a child forever'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: the line is Cicero's, at Orator section 120 (46 BC). The Latin is long public domain; this English rendering's translator is unidentified.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, orator and philosopher
answer.sourceLine: Cicero wrote it, and the locator is narrower than most sites say. The sentence sits in Orator — his last book on rhetoric, finished late in 46 BC and addressed to Marcus Junius Brutus — at section 120, in a passage urging the ideal speaker to learn history as well as law. The Latin, confirmed in the text on Latin Wikisource ↗, reads Nescire autem quid ante quam natus sis acciderit, id est semper esse puerum — literally “to not know what happened before you were born, that is to be always a boy.” The translator of the popular English wording is unidentified, which is a separate question from whether Cicero wrote the thought: he did.

source.excerpt: Not to know what happened before you were born is to be a child forever. For what is the time of a man, except it be interwoven with that memory of ancient things of a previous age?
trail: The Latin sentence sits between the section markers for 120 and 121 in the full Latin text of Orator on Latin Wikisource ↗, immediately after Cicero’s praise of Atticus for compressing seven hundred years of record into one book.
Wikiquote’s sourced Cicero page ↗ files this exact English wording under Orator Ad M. Brutum (46 BC) at section 120 — the same work and the same locator as the Latin above.

Wikipedia’s article on the Orator ↗ dates the work to the latter part of 46 BC and describes it as the continuation of a debate with Brutus begun in Brutus, written earlier the same year — two different books, one year, one dedicatee, which is how the citations get swapped.

Watson’s nineteenth-century Bohn volume Cicero on Oratory and Orators ↗ prints De Oratore and Brutus in full. A full-text search of it does not return this sentence, because the Orator is not among the treatises that volume contains.
source.excerptNote: The second sentence is part of the same thought and is almost always dropped when the line is quoted. Both sentences are rendered here as Wikiquote’s sourced Cicero page ↗ gives them.

source.rightsNote: Cicero’s Latin is unquestionably in the public domain — he died in 43 BC. The English wording shown is a different matter: no source consulted names its translator or the edition it came from, so quotle.info asserts no rights status for it rather than guessing. The public-domain English editions of Cicero’s rhetorical works that are easiest to find (Watson’s Bohn volume, linked above) contain De Oratore and Brutus but not the Orator, which is part of why this sentence circulates without a named translator.

author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (3 January 106 BC – 7 December 43 BC) was Rome’s most celebrated advocate and, in the Republic’s last decades, one of its most exposed politicians. He wrote the Orator in 46 BC, with Caesar in power and his own political life effectively over, turning back to the craft he had spent his career practising in the courts. He was killed on the proscription lists three years later.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Cicero wrote this. What travels wrongly is where it comes from and who put it into English — so this section is a citation fact-check, not a debunk.

items.why: Quotation sites routinely cite the line as Brutus, chapter 34, section 120. Brutus and Orator are two separate treatises, both written in 46 BC and both addressed to Marcus Junius Brutus — Wikipedia notes that the Orator continues a debate begun in Brutus ↗. The sentence is in the Orator.

Others give De Oratore, an earlier and much longer dialogue from 55 BC, sometimes describing it as “another name for” the Orator. It is not. Watson’s Bohn translation ↗ prints De Oratore complete, and this sentence is not in it.

The English wording in circulation is nobody’s identified translation. It is not Loeb’s and it matches none of the public-domain versions checked here, so quotle.info names no translator and claims no copyright status for the English.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Cicero’s, written late in 46 BC at Orator 120 — verifiable in the Latin ↗. The work is the Orator, not Brutus and not De Oratore.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cicero is not making a general point about education here. He is listing what a complete public speaker has to carry in his head, and he has just finished insisting the man know civil law, because — as Cicero asks — what is more disgraceful than taking on a legal case while being ignorant of the law? History is the next item on the list.

The compliment that sets it up is to his friend Atticus, who had squeezed seven hundred years of Roman record into a single book and so, Cicero says, lightened the work for everyone. The famous sentence is the reason that book matters: a man who knows nothing before his own birth has only his own lifetime to think with.
detailsBody: The Orator was written in the latter part of 46 BC, three years before Cicero was killed, and is his last word on rhetoric. It answers a request from Marcus Junius Brutus — the same Brutus — and continues an argument the two had started in Brutus earlier that year.

That shared dedicatee and shared year are the whole reason this quotation is so often filed under the wrong title. The two books sit next to each other in editions, in catalogues and in the same breath, and a section number copied from one lands plausibly in the other.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Latin sentence "Nescire autem quid ante quam natus sis acciderit, id est semper esse puerum" appears in Cicero’s Orator between section markers 120 and 121.
Wikiquote files this exact English wording under Cicero’s Orator Ad M. Brutum (46 BC), section 120, together with the following sentence about the time of a man.
Orator was written in the latter part of 46 BC, is Cicero’s last work on rhetoric, and continues a debate with Marcus Junius Brutus begun in Brutus earlier the same year.
Watson’s Bohn volume Cicero on Oratory and Orators contains De Oratore and Brutus, and its full text does not contain this sentence.
